title: Team members & end users
blurb: Tell apart the people who build the outputs from the people who will use them, and know what each is responsible for.
question: A warehouse is getting a new scanning system. Developers build it, a trainer writes the guides, and the pickers will use it every shift. Who are the team members, who are the end users, and what should each group do?

teach.body: Two groups are easy to confuse in exam questions. Project team members are the people who carry out the work: they deliver the work packages that produce the outputs. End users are the people who will use those outputs once they are handed over, usually in business as usual (BAU). One group builds the new thing; the other has to live and work with it afterwards.

rows.label: Who they are
values: People who will use the outputs

rows.label: Report to / via
values: Senior user rep on the board

teach.caption: On iterative projects a product owner also represents users' interests day to day.

teach.h: Why end users make or break benefits
teach.body: A project delivers outputs, but benefits only come when people use those outputs and change how they work. A new system nobody adopts produces no benefit at all. That is why end users provide requirements early, help test and accept the outputs, and then adopt the change in BAU. By doing so they enable the benefits that the sponsor is accountable for.

teach.body: Kestrel Logistics is replacing paper pick-lists with handheld scanners. The team members are two developers, a network engineer and a trainer: they estimate their work, build and test the system and report to the project manager. When the engineer spots weak Wi-Fi in the cold store, she raises it as a risk. The end users are the pickers: they explain how picking really works, try the prototype, accept the final system and then use it every shift.

rows.label: Estimating effort for a work package
Raising a risk with the project manager

teach.caption: Team members test to check quality; end users test to confirm the outputs work for them before accepting.

teach.text: Exam distractors give these groups other people's jobs: team members 'owning the business case' or 'approving gates', end users 'controlling the budget and schedule'. Team members DO the work and report to the PM; end users USE the outputs, accept them and adopt them. Neither owns budgets, benefits or decisions.

items: Team members carry out the work and deliver work packages, providing specialist expertise and estimates.
Team members report progress to the project manager and help identify risks and issues.
End users are the people who will use the outputs: they provide requirements and help test and accept them.
End users adopt the change in BAU, which is what enables the benefits.

summary: You can now describe what project team members and end users are each responsible for, tell them apart in a scenario, and explain why end users' involvement and adoption are essential for benefits to be realised.

A.q: Which role carries out the work that delivers a project's work packages?
A.why: Project team members carry out the work and deliver the work packages, using their specialist expertise.

whyNot.1: End users use the outputs; they do not build them.
whyNot.2: The sponsor is accountable at a senior level and does not deliver work packages.
whyNot.3: The governance board directs the project and makes key decisions.

A.q: Who are a project's end users?
options: The people who fund the project
The specialists who build the outputs
The people who will use the outputs
The office that sets the standards
A.why: End users are the people who will use the project's outputs, usually in business as usual after handover.

whyNot.0: Funding is secured by the sponsor.
whyNot.1: The specialists who build outputs are project team members.
whyNot.3: Standards are set and supported by a PMO.

A.q: Which of the following is a responsibility of end users?
A.why: End users help test the outputs and accept them, confirming they meet their needs.

whyNot.0: The project manager prepares the schedule.
whyNot.1: The sponsor owns the business case, and approval sits with the sponsor and governance board.
whyNot.2: Estimates come from the project manager and team members.

B.q: A team member spots that a key component might arrive late. What should they do?
options: Raise it with the project manager
Wait to see if it really does happen
Quietly change the design to fit
B.why: Team members help identify risks and issues by raising them with the project manager, who can log, assess and respond.

whyNot.0: Going straight to the sponsor bypasses the project manager, who manages risks within tolerance.
whyNot.2: A possible future problem is a risk; it should be raised early, not left until it happens.
whyNot.3: Changing the design without authority bypasses change control.

B.q:
Which TWO of the following are typical responsibilities of project team members?
1) Providing estimates for their own work
2) Owning the business case
3) Reporting progress to the project manager
4) Prioritising the product backlog
B.why: Team members provide estimates for their work (1) and report progress to the project manager (3).

whyNot.0: Owning the business case (2) is the sponsor's responsibility.
whyNot.1: Prioritising the backlog (4) is the product owner's responsibility.
whyNot.2: Neither 2 nor 4 is a team member responsibility.

B.q: Why do end users matter so much to benefits realisation?
options: Benefits need outputs to be used
They approve each of the decision gates
B.why: Benefits only arise when the outputs are adopted and used. End users' adoption of the change enables the benefits.

whyNot.1: The sponsor secures funding, not end users.
whyNot.2: Gate approval is a governance decision for the sponsor or board.
whyNot.3: The project manager writes the project management plan.

C.q: A bank's new mortgage app is complete and accepted, but branch staff keep using the old paper forms. Which responsibility is most clearly not being met?
C.why: The outputs exist, but the people meant to use them have not adopted the change in BAU, so the benefits cannot be realised.

whyNot.0: The app has been built and accepted, so delivery of the work has happened.
whyNot.1: PMO standards are not the cause of staff refusing to use a finished system.
whyNot.3: Planning has already led to a delivered output; the gap is in adoption.

C.q: Which of the following is NOT normally a responsibility of a project team member?
options: Helping to identify risks and issues
C.why: Accepting outputs on behalf of the business is done by end users (and, on iterative work, the product owner), not by the team that built them.

whyNot.0: Delivering work packages is the core of a team member's role.
whyNot.2: Team members are there for their specialist expertise.
whyNot.3: Team members help the project manager identify risks and issues.

C.q: Before a new medication system is designed, ward nurses are asked to describe how they record drug rounds. What role are the nurses playing?
C.why: The nurses will use the system, so they are end users, and describing their needs is providing requirements.

whyNot.1: The nurses are not building the system; the project team does that.
whyNot.2: Securing funding is the sponsor's role.
whyNot.3: Assurance is a PMO function and has nothing to do with describing ward routines.

reteach.title: The kitchen fitters and the family who cook there
reteach.question: A family has a new kitchen fitted. Who are the 'team members' and who are the 'end users', and what does each need to do for the kitchen to be a success?

blocks.body: The fitter, electrician and plumber are the team members: they each do their part, tell the kitchen company how long it will take and flag problems like a hidden pipe. The family are the end users: they say where the hob and dishwasher must go, check everything works before signing off and then cook there every day. A beautiful kitchen the family won't use has delivered nothing.

blocks.text: Signing off the kitchen is the family's call, not the fitters'. In projects, end users accept the outputs; team members deliver them.

explain.body: Team members are the specialists who carry out the project work and deliver the work packages. They provide expertise and estimates for their part of the job.

test.q: Which best describes a project team member?
options: A senior manager who funds it
A person who uses outputs in BAU
test.why: A team member is a specialist who carries out project work and delivers work packages.

whyNot.0: The senior person who secures funding is the sponsor.
whyNot.1: People who use the outputs in BAU are end users.
whyNot.2: Gate approval belongs to the sponsor and governance board.

explain.body: Team members report progress to the project manager and help identify risks and issues, raising them early so the project manager can act.

test.q: To whom do project team members normally report progress?
test.why: Team members report progress to the project manager, who leads the team day to day.

whyNot.0: The board receives reports from the project manager via the sponsor.
whyNot.1: End users are not the team's reporting line.
whyNot.3: The PMO may collect reports from project managers but does not manage the team.

explain.body: End users provide requirements, help test the outputs and accept them, confirming the outputs are fit for the way they actually work.

test.q: At which point do end users formally confirm the outputs meet their needs?
options: When the project funding is secured
test.why: End users confirm the outputs meet their needs when they accept them, usually after acceptance testing.

whyNot.0: Funding is secured by the sponsor before outputs even exist.
whyNot.2: Estimating happens during planning, before anything has been built.
whyNot.3: Resource levelling is a scheduling technique for the project manager.

explain.body: After handover, end users adopt the change in BAU. Their real use of the outputs is what enables the benefits the sponsor is accountable for.

test.q: After handover, what must end users do for the benefits to be realised?
test.why: Benefits come from using the outputs, so end users must adopt the change in their everyday work.

whyNot.1: The issue log is managed by the project manager.
whyNot.2: Gate approval is for the sponsor or governance board.
whyNot.3: The sponsor owns the business case, written long before handover.
